issues.title: matching  specifics and wording for the difference in checking permitted vs excluded
issues.author: bob-beck
issues.body:
Section 3.6 phrases permitted subtree matching as 'use RFC 9525 §6.3 excluding wildcard semantics.' 

This is concise but potentially harder to parse than 'treat the wildcard label as a literal label' or 'strip the wildcard label before matching.'

I think this is the equivalent with less repetition from 9525 the way I have it, but I may be wrong.  

very happy for thoughts on better wording.

issues.title: Should this even see the light of day?
issues.author: bob-beck
issues.body:
I wrote it all down because I was annoyed, and outline the why this way in the alternatives. 

If there's a reasonable way to fix the existing stuff and *somehow* reliably gate on upcoming "new" changes, I'm all ears but I have not pondered that myself. 

Obviously, if we're only worried about this for a PLANTS/MTC type certificate in the future, we could attempt to gate something on support of that and we don't care about legacy goo, but it's not clear to me that there's a clean way to do that, and that it would even matter - frankly using wildcards in the public web pki should probably just die and then the problem becomes irrelevant.

So I'm still on the cleanest way to provide a way is to use a new oid.  A CA that cares includes it and it has to be supported. 

But I'd love a simpler way :)

issues.author: bob-beck
issues.body:
Yes, it's a number pulled from thin air

Possibly based on experience and what I've seen in the world but nevertheless a bum number.

Happy to entertain different values here within reason, but believe that given this is only a restriction
when used in combination with an extension that the CA would be making a choice to use, we want to
limit what can be here to something that makes this not a denial of service vector.

pulls.title: Improve restrictions on expanding constraints
pulls.author: bob-beck
pulls.body:
After a discussion with David Benjamin, I was reminded of the better way to do this.

In this manner a chain builder can enforce each step, but the leaf need only be checked against it's signer.

comments.author: ounsworth
comments.body:
So, this is doing a philosophically weird thing in that now I'm not sure where the enforcement point is to catch sub CAs that are misbehaving by containing an invalid EENR extn.

The kicker is that these two sentences in the new diff seem contradictory:

> 193 no walking of the certification path is
> 194 required.


> 213 A verifier MUST reject any certification path whose CA certificates
> 214 do not satisfy these propagation rules.

How is the verifier supposed to reject a CA that does not satisfy these propagation rules if it is not required to walk the certification path?
You can't have you cake an eat it too.

If you're trying to do what you're trying to do, then you should suggest a GREASE-like random check or a check-on-first-use model.

GREASE-like would be:

> In order to catch mis-issued CAs that do not satisfy these propagation rules, verifiers SHOULD sporadically walk a certification path to ensure compliance; for example full path validation could be performed randomly with a low probability.

Check-on-first-use would be something like:

> A client SHOULD perform a full path validation check for conformance with these propagation rules the first time it sees a particular intermediate CA certificate and MAY then cache that intermediate certificate in such a way that future encounters do not require re-checking. Alternatively, verifiers MAY skip the path propagation check entirely if it has assurance that the intermediate CAs are being externally audited.

`permittedSubtrees` MUST be contained, in the sense of {{RFC5280}}
section 4.2.1.10, in some entry of the issuer's `permittedSubtrees`.

Referencing 5280::4.2.1.10 is fine, but can you please inline the salient bit so that this paragraph is self-contained. Maybe:

> ... the 'permittedSubtrees' list MUST be equal to or a subset of the 'permittedSubtrees' list in its issuer's certificate. That means every entry in the issued CA's
`permittedSubtrees` MUST be contained, in the sense of {{RFC5280}}
section 4.2.1.10, in some entry of the issuer's `permittedSubtrees`. Entries that appear in the issuer's certificate MAY be dropped from the list in the issued certificate in order to restrict the list.

pulls.title: Add the alternative of putting these defintions in 5280
pulls.author: bob-beck
pulls.body:
Using a critical extension as a marker that they are supported, and solving the wildcard problem that way.

Only gets to solve the name constraint problem, not tag on other improvements to the name constraint processing. 

(and requires us to rev 5280)

Suggested by a chat with David Benjamin

comments.author: ounsworth
comments.body:
Let me get this straight -- you're saying to trash the thing defined in this document, and add a critical flag extension whose presence changes the processing rules of 5280's NameConstraints extn. That's certainly "Updates 5280", not "Amends 5280".

I could see an approach like that -- maybe -- if the flag ext was non-critical so that the same cert was simultaneously valid to old clients under the old rules and to new clients under the new rules, but without the backwards-compat goal, that just seems messy for no gain?

I assume you would eventually pick one or the other and not leave both in the document?

comments.author: bob-beck
comments.body:
No, the point of being able to add the critical flag is to get what you otherwise only get with the new critical extension, the ability of the CA to decide "hey I really want to meaningfully restrict this key with excluded subtrees, and It might sign wildcards - and I don't want anything it signs accepted by any client that doesn't understand the wildcard semantics for name constraints". 

Effectively, it's a hacky way to tie the update to the name constraint behaviour to the update of 5280, instead of making a new "name constraint like" thing for TLS, that still preserves the property of "a way for CA's to know it will be enforced". 

If let's say the wildcard in dns name constraint behavoiur was actually spec'ed in RFC 5280 bis 27, you could think of the extension as effectively meaning "you understand this extension only of you are conformant to 5280 bis 27 - aka I require you to understand 5280 bis 27 to corrrectly deal with this certificate".

comments.author: bob-beck
comments.body: and yes, for the purpose of this document, we're not picking that alternative, but for the purpose of a discussion in lamps or whatever, mention it and the differences.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
I talked a bit with @rolandshoemaker, who has also been spending a lot of time with name constraints recently, and I think I prefer this approach.

So, ultimately, the problem here is that a DNS excludedSubtree, as described in RFC 5280, is basically broken. Faced with relying parties that implement RFC 5280 and wildcard DNS SANs, it is not possible for a CA to express a DNS excludedSubtree in a way that means anything. An excludedSubtree of `foo.example.com` *should* have forbidden a SAN of `*.example.com`, but it does not. Some X.509 software got this right anyway, but most did not until recently. (There's also silliness where DNS wildcard SANs, in practice implemented at the X.509 layer, is only specified in RFC 9525.)

To fix this, we could either:

1. Define a second name constraints extension, fix this, and bundle in any other name constraint improvements we might want. Get relying parties to implement this extension. Use criticality to block older relying parties.

2. Update RFC 5280 to tighten the semantics of this particular issue, punt bigger name constraint fixes. Get relying parties to implement the new semantics. This is not gated on a flag or anything, we say you should ship an update to fix this spec bug. (Several verifiers have already done this. I know some that have done this for years.) Use a separate requireWildcardAwareNameConstraints extension to block older relying parties.

The cost of (1) is we'll basically have two name constraints extensions indefinitely. I don't think relying parties will be able to drop support for name constraints v1.

The cost of (2) is we have to deal with the ambiguity of whether RPs have the fixed or broken semantics, and we don't get to apply any of the bigger fixes, because we have to stay generally compatible.

I do have many gripes with name constraints. (Roland and I have a write-up to publish on how to check them without it becoming an O(N^2) DoS vector.) But they're mostly of the performance/DoS variety, and (1) doesn't actually help with those. As long as relying parties have to implement the first name constraints, the DoS vector is there and we need to figure out how to implement it efficiently. So I'm not offended by having to punt bigger fixes, at least right now. (We can always introduce name constraints v2 later.) And, all else equal, I'd rather have one variant of the extension to implement than two.

Regarding compatibility, the two approaches give you the same tools. There are three categories of RPs, not two:

a. Relying parties that implement RFC 5280 today
b. Relying parties that implement the fixed semantics today
c. Relying parties that implement whatever new critical extension defined in (1) and (2)

As a CA that wishes to express a DNS excludedSubtree, you have to deal with the fact that category (a) cannot enforce your constraint correctly. Categories (b) and (c) are fine. But you can't distinguish (a) and (b) by criticality. You can either:

**Fail closed and have (a) reject your certificates**

If you want to fail closed:
1. In design (1), use critical nameConstraintsV2
2. In design (2), use critical nameConstraints and critical requireWildcardAwareNameConstraints

In both cases, you lose compatibility with (a) and also lose compatibility with (b), even though (b) would actually have been fine.

**Fail open and have (a) accept your certificates, _even though your constraint isn't enforced_**

If you want to fail open:
1. In design (1), use non-critical nameConstraintsV2 and equivalent critical nameConstraintsV1 extension
2. In design (2), use critical nameConstraints and don't include requireWildcardAwareNameConstraints

In both cases, you keep compatibility with (a) and (b) but your constraint will not be enforced by (a). In design (1), you end up doubling up the constraint.

**Assume (a) doesn't exist**

You might know all your RPs are new enough:
* Maybe you're a more controled deployment and can make sure your RPs are all updated past some hotfix
* Maybe it's been 10 years since this document is published and you can reasonably assume everyone's fixed their verifiers
* Maybe you're a CA that uses some new algorithm and that puts a lower bound on the age of the verifier software

If you don't have to worry about (a), then you can pick the simplest option:
1. In design (1), use critical nameConstraintsV2
2. In design (2), use critical nameConstraints and don't include requireWildcardAwareNameConstraints

But here the simplest option for design (1) sacrifices RPs in category (b).

---

So we actually just get the same capabilities in both. We update RFC 5280 to tell RPs to implement the new behavior. That starts the trasition clock. Mid-transition, requireWildcardAwareNameConstraints is available for folks who want to fail closed (at the cost of breaking more stuff), but in the future, CAs can stop needing to include it.

While this does not give an opportunity to make big, incompatible changes to name constraints, it gives us an opportunity to clarify other things:

* The core semantics of DNS wildcards should move from 9525 to 5280
* Edge cases of email and URI name constraints are a bit underspecified right now
* Maybe we write down how to check name constraints without it being a DoS vector...

comments.author: bob-beck
comments.body:
your last three points sum up the bulk of my gripes. 


fundamentally, I have written this down on the assumption it would be not be wanted to rev 5280 for this, particularly the key thing in my mind being that the possibly "changing" semantics of a 5280 defined critical extension by nebulous external factors are the core problem 

The other improvements are simply to not waste the opportunity if we are solving it this way. 

So I am fine with either approach (although I think for purposes of this doc that means I should merge this pr)

comments.author: ounsworth
comments.body:
Ultimately, I'm ok with either option too. @davidben makes all good points.

I am somewhat attracted by the simplifications that Bob's EENR does not apply to CNs and does not apply to the CA certs themselves. But those might not be enough of a win to justify a whole new thing.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
Oh yeah, definitely on board with exploring what we'd put in a new name constraints if we wanted to. I'm leaning towards it probably not being worth it, but maybe there'll be enough worthwhile incompatible changes to justify it.

(Though I do think, whether or not v2 exists, it's prudent to change RPs to interpret v1 in a way that fixes the excludedSubtrees. The existing semantics are clearly just wrong, and the fix won't break anything.)

comments.body: I guess the "fix v1" path leads to eventually filing CVEs against all the clients that still parse it wrong -- which one could argue is the correct path.
